1: # Unfinished Business
2: 
3: **Turn unfinished ideas into hackathon-ready builds.**
4: 
5: Unfinished Business is an OpenCode-powered hackathon project builder. Four friendly spirits guide one idea through a clear proposal, an approved plan, a real bounded build, and evidence you can defend.
6: 
7: ![Ghostlight Hacker Workshop landing page](tests/visual/snapshots/landing-wide.png)
8: 
9: ## What it is
10: 
11: - A **landing page** at `/` built around the hero, the four-stage workflow, one sample project, why OpenCode does the coding, local setup and privacy, and a short FAQ.
12: - A **guided sample** at `/demo`: one versioned Driftwatch fixture — an abandoned open-source CLI revived through clarification, a plan, one bounded change, a recorded check, and Witness findings. It has Play/Pause, step, replay, reset, four inspectable spirit tabs, and an optional 90-second presentation mode at `/demo?presentation=1`. It does not call a model or read a repository.
13: - The **real workshop** at `/workshop`, which connects to a local OpenCode server and records what actually happened.
14: - A **first-run connection and discovery flow** that checks a supported OpenCode server, lists the models/providers/agents it actually reports, and lets the builder choose a model and reported reasoning variant. Provider API keys stay inside OpenCode.
15: - A **read-only hosted sample** and a **private hosted** mode. Neither reaches into a visitor's local repository.
16: - A versioned **schema v7** contract for explicit project sources, field-level Oracle intake answers, structured facts/decisions/assumptions with editable superseding corrections, structured proposals, reviewable candidate section revisions, model preferences, provider errors, and recoverable operations. Explicit v1–v6 migrations keep older projects usable.
17: - **Reviewable Architect revisions**: every section has a content contract; a change request generates a candidate with a summary and complete Markdown draft. The user inspects a unified or side-by-side diff, then accepts, requests another revision, or discards. Only an accepted candidate replaces the current draft, and approval remains a separate exact-version action.
18: - **Focused workshop**: one primary task at a time, a collapsible project outline, a contextual Activity & results drawer, an editable Project memory drawer, and a compact model/connection header. Empty technical panels no longer occupy permanent space.
19: - **Activity & results**: the former Run Inspector is organized into Progress, Changes, and Checks. Native IDs, capability mappings, raw evidence, provider payloads, and the transcript stay under Technical details or Advanced diagnostics.
20: - **Editable project memory**: decisions, user answers, assumptions, constraints, and unresolved questions are visible in one place. A correction supersedes the prior entry without changing an approval, section draft, Maker scope, or native run.
21: - **Focused, multi-turn Oracle discovery**: every fresh project chooses new work, a validated local repository, a credential-free remote repository import, or saved work before discovery. Oracle asks at most three explained questions per turn and proposes only after essential intake is known or the user explicitly accepts stated assumptions.
22: - **Observable, cancellable, recoverable runs**: every Oracle, Architect, Maker, and Witness run is a persisted asynchronous operation with live progress phases, elapsed time, and Continue waiting / Reconcile / Open in OpenCode / Cancel / Retry / Mark abandoned controls in Activity & results. A timed-out or restarted run never permanently blocks the project; reconciliation retrieves and validates the actual late response or diff and applies it exactly once.
23: 
24: OpenCode supplies the agent loop, model access, native tools, permissions, execution, interruption, and native sessions. Unfinished Business adds the four-stage workshop, exact-version approvals, dependency invalidation, evidence views, the onboarding/discovery flow, and the Ghostlight interface. It does **not** ship a second coding harness or a general command executor.
25: 
26: | Spirit | Role |
27: |---|---|
28: | Oracle | Choose the project source, collect structured answers over focused turns, and prepare a fact/decision/assumption-aware proposal |
29: | Architect | Draft one planning section and wait for approval of that exact version |
30: | Maker | Perform an approved, bounded native edit through OpenCode |
31: | Witness | Inspect evidence in a fresh session and prepare honest review drafts |
32: 
33: ## Runtime modes
34: 
35: **Hosted sample** — `UB_DEPLOYMENT_MODE=hosted-demo`. A public, read-only sample. It has no OpenCode process, provider credentials, session token, visitor persistence, or repository access. Every non-GET `/api/*` request returns `403 DEMO_READ_ONLY`.
36: 
37: **Private hosted** — `REDACTED`. A password-protected Render or self-hosted instance with a private disk and a loopback OpenCode child. Maker edits the server's isolated demo workspace. A hosted browser cannot edit a visitor's machine.
38: 
39: **Local workshop** — `UB_DEPLOYMENT_MODE=local` (default). The browser app, local API, and pinned OpenCode server run on the builder's machine over loopback. Oracle source onboarding validates local directories and can import a public HTTPS repository into an app-managed workspace after explicit confirmation. Maker's edit remains bounded to the isolated demo workspace; selecting a source does not authorize implementation in that repository.

133: ## Status and limitations
134: 
135: The prior release phases remain integrated. **Phase 8** adds the final hardening gate: an end-to-end workshop journey test, responsive snapshots at 390/768/1440, loading/offline/long-content checks, accessible revision tabs and live progress announcements, broader security route tests, a zero-advisory dependency audit, and in-repository hackathon copy/assets. **Platform Phase 7** adds macOS support alongside the existing Linux x64 path: the official cross-platform `@opencode/cli` replaces the Linux-only package, runtime resolution prefers a compatible global `opencode` then the lockfile binary, and CI runs `41252770576` and `41253037115` passed Linux x64, macOS Apple Silicon, and macOS Intel. Upgrade Phase 6 rewrites the public story around one canonical Driftwatch sample. Upgrade Phase 5 remains the focused workshop. Schema v7 is unchanged.
136: 
137: Known limitations:
138: 
139: - The application is a trusted single-project tool, not a multi-tenant sandbox. Remote imports are public HTTPS clones into a managed local directory; private/authenticated repositories, shared-host isolation, arbitrary Maker access to selected repositories, and remote browser-to-local pairing remain deferred.
140: - The supported local hosts are **Linux x64**, **macOS Apple Silicon**, and **macOS Intel**, verified by local runs and CI runs `41252770576`/`41253037115`. Windows, Linux ARM64, and 32-bit hosts are unsupported.
141: - Maker edits only `UB_DATA_DIR/demo-workspace`; the Node check is not an OS sandbox.
142: - Generated section review supports a deliberately small, safe Markdown subset (headings, paragraphs, lists, emphasis, links, tables, and code), not full CommonMark or raw HTML. Contract validation checks structure and topic coverage, not prose quality.
143: - Model availability, pricing, quota, training terms, and billing are controlled by OpenCode/provider. The spending limit only checks cost OpenCode reports after a session; unknown-price providers may bill before that value is visible.
144: - The workspace privacy preference records intent; the app cannot attest every provider's training/retention contract. Provider rejections that mention training/data policy are explained as `PROVIDER_DATA_POLICY`.
145: - Advanced diagnostics load only when opened. Permission polling is best-effort; a pending request remains visible in Activity & results and the contextual permission alert, but a provider-side change can lag by one refresh interval.
146: - Backboard is not integrated and no partner category is claimed for installation alone. Sentry is configured but live release/source-map/trace verification requires authorized credentials and a deployment.
147: - No public hosted URL, recorded video, published article, or submission is asserted by this repository.
148: - A real recorded demonstration and final submission packaging remain separate acceptance work.

1: # Hackathon and release copy
2: 
3: **Status:** Prepared in-repository. No external submission, publication, deployment, or video upload has been performed.
4: **Owner:** Engineering/release.
5: **Last verified:** 2026-11-01.
6: 
7: Use this copy only with the limitations below. Do not add testimonials, user counts, awards, benchmark numbers, or live-provider claims that are not in `docs/EVIDENCE.md`.
8: 
9: ## One-line pitch
10: 
11: Unfinished Business is an OpenCode-powered workshop that helps a builder finish one stalled hackathon project through a clear plan, an approved build, and evidence they can defend.
12: 
13: ## Short description (about 50 words)
14: 
15: Unfinished Business turns one unfinished idea into a reviewable plan, a bounded OpenCode build, and honest evidence. Four stages keep the human in charge: Oracle clarifies, Architect drafts, Maker edits an isolated workspace with explicit approval, and Witness reports what actually ran — including what did not.
16: 
17: ## Longer description
18: 
19: Hackathon projects rarely fail at the idea. They fail at the gap between an appealing pitch and a build someone can verify.
20: 
21: Unfinished Business is a local-first workshop built around OpenCode. The Oracle asks a few focused questions and stores answers with provenance. The Architect drafts one section at a time against a content contract; revisions are previewed and accepted separately from approval. Maker runs only after every section and a separate scope statement are approved, and it edits an isolated demo workspace rather than an arbitrary repository. Witness reviews the observed diff and bounded Node check in a fresh session. The screen reports live progress, pending permissions, and recoverable failures without inventing a successful run.
22: 
23: The public `/demo` route is a recorded Driftwatch sample. It is labeled as recorded and makes no model or repository call. The live workshop uses the builder's own OpenCode 2.x server; provider keys never enter the browser or this application.
24: 
25: ## Built with
26: 
27: - TypeScript, React 19, Vite 8, and Hono
28: - OpenCode 2.0.32 through `@opencode/client` and the cross-platform `@opencode/cli`
29: - Zod contracts, an atomic JSON project store, and a bounded Node test check
30: - Playwright for visual, responsive, keyboard, contrast, zoom, and offline checks
31: - Optional Sentry error/trace instrumentation with metadata-only redaction
32: 
33: ## Demo script (90 seconds)
34: 
35: The full beat map is in [docs/DEMO_AND_SUBMISSION.md](../DEMO_AND_SUBMISSION.md).
36: 
37: 1. Open `/` and state the problem: unfinished projects, not missing ideas.
38: 2. Open `/demo` and label it as the recorded Driftwatch sample.
39: 3. Step through Oracle clarification, Architect approval, Maker's bounded change, the recorded check, and Witness findings.
40: 4. Point out that the live session remains `NOT_RUN`; the sample is not evidence of live inference.
41: 5. Open `/workshop`, show source selection and the OpenCode connection panel, and stop before any claim that a live provider call occurred.
42: 6. Close on the evidence view and the limitation statement.
43: 
44: ## Claim checklist
45: 
46: | Claim | Evidence | Limit |
47: |---|---|---|
48: | Four-stage workflow with separate approvals | `tests/workflow.test.ts`, `tests/experience.test.ts`, `tests/journey.test.ts` | App approval is not tool permission |
49: | Reviewable Architect revisions | `tests/revisions.test.ts`, `tests/web.test.ts`, `tests/visual/snapshots/` | Markdown subset, not full CommonMark |
50: | Recoverable async runs | `tests/observable-runs.test.ts`, `tests/experience-hardening.test.ts`, `tests/journey.test.ts` | No automatic retry; reconciliation is explicit |
51: | OpenCode owns provider credentials | `docs/OPENCODE_INTEGRATION.md`, `tests/connection.test.ts`, `tests/web.test.ts` | Provider terms are not attested by the app |
52: | Linux and macOS support | CI runs `41252770576` and `41253037115`; `docs/LOCAL_SETUP.md` | Windows and Linux ARM64 unsupported |
53: | Recorded sample is not live proof | `src/shared/demo.ts`, `tests/demo.test.ts`, `tests/visual/demo.spec.ts` | Live native session remains `NOT_RUN` |
54: 
55: ## Asset manifest
56: 
57: Canonical assets are committed; do not generate replacement screenshots for a submission without inspecting them.
58: 
59: | Asset | Path | Use |
60: |---|---|---|
61: | Wide landing capture | `tests/visual/snapshots/landing-wide.png` | README hero, project gallery |
62: | Tablet landing capture | `tests/visual/snapshots/landing-tablet.png` | Responsive proof |
63: | Narrow landing capture | `tests/visual/snapshots/landing-narrow.png` | Mobile proof |
64: | Wide workshop capture | `tests/visual/snapshots/workshop-wide.png` | Real workshop |
65: | Tablet onboarding capture | `tests/visual/snapshots/onboarding-tablet.png` | Setup/responsive proof |
66: | Guided sample wide | `tests/visual/snapshots/demo-guided-wide.png` | Recorded sample |
67: | Guided sample presentation | `tests/visual/snapshots/demo-presentation-wide.png` | 90-second path |
68: | Activity & results | `tests/visual/snapshots/run-inspector.png` | Recovery/evidence surface |
69: | Hero source master | `assets/source/hero-workshop-revival.webp` | Source provenance; not shipped |
70: | Responsive hero variants | `public/assets/hero/` | Shipped landing hero |
71: 
72: ## Submission checklist
73: 
74: - [ ] Re-run `npm run typecheck`, `npm test`, `npm run build`, `npm run budget`, `npm run test:visual`, `npm run test:platform`, and `npm run smoke:opencode`.
75: - [ ] Re-read `docs/EVIDENCE.md` and remove any claim without current evidence.
76: - [ ] Record and review the demo; label the recorded sample and the missing live proof.

78: - [ ] Publish only with separate explicit authorization.

Repository: /home/kernel-kain/Documents/Github/unfinished-business (branch main).
Prerequisite: Prompt 1 confirmed and approved spending.

Goal: the app runs its Oracle, Architect, Maker, and Witness stages on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (API id `deepseek-flash`), through OpenCode. The app never holds the provider key. OpenCode does.

Step 1: Verify the provider path before coding:
- Run `opencode --version` (the pinned version is 2.0.32) and find how OpenCode 2.x configures a provider: its config file, how it accepts a base URL and an API key, and how it names the DeepSeek provider. Read `opencode --help` and the OpenCode docs for the installed version. Do not guess the config key names.
- Confirm the DeepSeek endpoint with one curl using a real key (base https://api.deepseek.com, model `deepseek-flash`). Keep the key in the environment only. Never write it to a file in the repo.
- Note: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash weights (552B) are not runnable on a laptop. The local run uses the DeepSeek API unless I approve an alternative. Do not claim a fully offline run unless it is tested.

Step 2: Configure OpenCode, not the app:
- Create a project-level OpenCode config (for example opencode.jsonc under docs/ or a judge-config folder, whichever OpenCode reads) that defines the DeepSeek provider with the model `deepseek-flash` and reads the key from an environment variable such as DEEPSEEK_API_KEY. Use the exact syntax that OpenCode 2.0.32 supports (verify it).
- Set the app's model policy so the selected model is `deepseek-flash` by default. Keep the existing "free and local only" and "paid confirmation" rules: DeepSeek is paid, so the first use needs explicit confirmation in the app. Check src/server/opencode/discovery.ts and src/shared/modes.ts to see how a paid remote model is classified.

Step 3: Render:
- In render.yaml, add DEEPSEEK_API_KEY as `sync: false` (secret set in the Render dashboard). Point OPENCODE_CONFIG_HOME at the config from Step 2 (or copy it in the start helper).
- Keep REDACTED for the live instance.
- Do not put real keys in any file.

Step 4: Verify live (this is a real model call, so keep it small):
- Start OpenCode locally, then start the app (npm start), connect in the wizard, select deepseek-flash, and send one short Oracle message. Record the reply and the time.
- Run `scripts/opencode-smoke.ts` and `scripts/opencode-live-diagnostic.ts` if they still apply. Record results.

Step 5: Tests: add or update tests for the config generation, the model-policy classification of deepseek-flash as paid, and the redaction of the key in logs. Run `npm run typecheck`, `npm test`.

Commit: "feat(models): run the workshop on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash through OpenCode". Report the config path, the test result, and the live reply evidence path under /tmp/opencode/e2e/.

# Your First API Call

The DeepSeek API uses an API format compatible with OpenAI/Anthropic. By modifying the configuration, you can use the OpenAI/Anthropic SDK or softwares compatible with the OpenAI/Anthropic API to access the DeepSeek API.

| PARAM | VALUE |
| --- | --- |
| base\_url (OpenAI) | `https://api.deepseek.com` |
| base\_url (Anthropic) | `https://api.deepseek.com/anthropic` |
| api\_key | apply for an [API key](https://platform.deepseek.com/api_keys) |
| model | `deepseek-flash`(1) `deepseek-v4-pro` |

(1) Use `deepseek-flash` as the model name. It is now served by DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, and the calling method remains unchanged. The legacy names `deepseek-v4-flash` and `deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp` are still accepted, but the corresponding models have been retired; their requests are served by DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 and billed at the Flash price.

## Integrate with Agent Tools[​](#integrate-with-agent-tools "Direct link to Integrate with Agent Tools")

DeepSeek Harness is now in developer preview for agent harness developers worldwide. See the [DeepSeek Harness Guide](https://deepseek-harness.github.io/deepseek-harness/en/guide/quickstart) for details.

The DeepSeek API is supported by many popular AI agent and coding assistant tools. If you use tools like Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, or OpenCode, you can use DeepSeek as the backend model directly — no code required.

See the [Agent Integrations Guide](/quick_start/agent_integrations/claude_code) for details.

## Invoke The Chat API[​](#invoke-the-chat-api "Direct link to Invoke The Chat API")

Once you have obtained an API key, you can access the DeepSeek model using the following example scripts in the OpenAI API format. This is a non-stream example, you can set the `stream` parameter to `true` to get stream response.

For examples using the Anthropic API format, please refer to [Anthropic API](/guides/anthropic_api).

Before running these examples, set the `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` environment variable in your terminal to your API key.

- curl

- python

- nodejs

```
curl https://api.deepseek.com/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${DEEPSEEK_API_KEY}" \
  -d '{
        "model": "deepseek-flash",
        "messages": [
          {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
          {"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}
        ],
        "thinking": {"type": "enabled"},
        "reasoning_effort": "high",
        "stream": false
      }'
```

It's not the build or the OpenCode startup — it's the global `Sec-Fetch-Site` gate in `src/server/app.ts`:

```ts
const fetchSite = context.req.header("sec-fetch-site");
if (fetchSite && fetchSite !== "same-origin" && fetchSite !== "none") {
  return ... "Cross-site requests are not allowed." ... 403
}
```

Modern browsers set `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` on a **top-level navigation that started from another site** — which is exactly what happens when you click the deployed URL in the Render dashboard, a chat, an email, or any other site. The check rejected the document request itself, so the browser rendered the JSON error instead of the app. It also rejected `same-site`, so any sibling-subdomain link was blocked too.

I confirmed this against the live deployment:

- `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` + `Sec-Fetch-Mode: navigate` + `Sec-Fetch-Dest: document` on `/` → **403** `Cross-site requests are not allowed.`
- `Sec-Fetch-Site: none` (typing the URL into the address bar) → **401** Basic auth, i.e. the request is fine and reaches login.

So: clicking the link fails, typing it manually works. That's the tell.

The `HEAD / → 401` line in your logs is just Render's liveness probe hitting Basic auth (it reports as `INTERNAL_ERROR` only because `errorCode()` doesn't map HTTP exceptions); it is not the failure.

## Fix

I scoped the check so cross-site **top-level GET/HEAD document navigations to the app shell** are allowed, while cross-site API calls and sub-resource loads (scripts, images, fetches) stay blocked. CSRF protection is unchanged: mutations still require `application/json` plus the `x-ub-session-token`.

- `src/server/app.ts` — added `isAppShellNavigation()` and used it in the `Sec-Fetch-Site` gate.
- `tests/http-hardening.test.ts` — regression coverage: cross-site document navigation to `/` is not 403, while cross-site `/api/*` requests (even as a document) and cross-site `image` loads remain 403.

`npm test` passes 207/207 and `npm run typecheck` is clean.

It's not the build or the OpenCode startup — it's the global `Sec-Fetch-Site` gate in `src/server/app.ts`:

```ts
const fetchSite = context.req.header("sec-fetch-site");
if (fetchSite && fetchSite !== "same-origin" && fetchSite !== "none") {
  return ... "Cross-site requests are not allowed." ... 403
}
```

Modern browsers set `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` on a **top-level navigation that started from another site** — which is exactly what happens when you click the deployed URL in the Render dashboard, a chat, an email, or any other site. The check rejected the document request itself, so the browser rendered the JSON error instead of the app. It also rejected `same-site`, so any sibling-subdomain link was blocked too.

I confirmed this against the live deployment:

- `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` + `Sec-Fetch-Mode: navigate` + `Sec-Fetch-Dest: document` on `/` → **403** `Cross-site requests are not allowed.`
- `Sec-Fetch-Site: none` (typing the URL into the address bar) → **401** Basic auth, i.e. the request is fine and reaches login.

So: clicking the link fails, typing it manually works. That's the tell.

The `HEAD / → 401` line in your logs is just Render's liveness probe hitting Basic auth (it reports as `INTERNAL_ERROR` only because `errorCode()` doesn't map HTTP exceptions); it is not the failure.

## Fix

I scoped the check so cross-site **top-level GET/HEAD document navigations to the app shell** are allowed, while cross-site API calls and sub-resource loads (scripts, images, fetches) stay blocked. CSRF protection is unchanged: mutations still require `application/json` plus the `x-ub-session-token`.

- `src/server/app.ts` — added `isAppShellNavigation()` and used it in the `Sec-Fetch-Site` gate.
- `tests/http-hardening.test.ts` — regression coverage: cross-site document navigation to `/` is not 403, while cross-site `/api/*` requests (even as a document) and cross-site `image` loads remain 403.

`npm test` passes 207/207 and `npm run typecheck` is clean.

Given the scope covers local run plus the live Render URL with judge instructions, I'm planning to update the default port to 4310 consistently across config.ts, .env.example, vite.config.ts, README, LOCAL_SETUP, and setup.ts, then make `npm start` build first and print a single URL with an OpenCode reachability check.

For judge instructions, I'll add a "Judge quick start" section in README covering the one-command start, the URL, the OpenCode step, and the deployed Render URL with a note about Basic auth credentials that the user needs to decide on. The live Render deployment already works fine, so no changes needed there.

I checked that tests don't reference the old port 4200, so that's safe. Now I'm designing the start.ts preflight logic: checking if the port is free by attempting to listen on it, and if it's busy, using a system command to identify the process holding it before printing a clear error and exiting. I'm also adding a quick health check against the OpenCode base URL with a short timeout, printing a warning if it's unreachable.

For the port and OpenCode checks, I confirmed start.ts is distinct from the Render startup path, so these preflight checks only affect local `npm start`/`dev` usage, which is correct. I'll also add a simple printed URL message when running in local mode so judges know where to open the browser, using plain stdout output rather than the structured JSON logging the rest of the app uses. The npm start script already chains the vite build step before launching the server, and building without a Sentry auth token should still work fine since it did before.

Now I'm writing the updated start.ts: wrapping config loading and the new preflight logic (checking if the port is free by probing it with a temporary server, plus pinging OpenCode's health endpoint) inside the existing try/catch, after the Sentry instrumentation import but before anything that depends on config being valid.

I decide a response status under 500 counts as reachable since even an auth failure means the server is listening, and I only need this check in local mode since hosted deployments spawn the server themselves. I'm organizing these checks into a separate launch-check module for testability, planning small tests for port and reachability detection, then sketching the start.ts flow that loads config and verifies the port is free before launching in local mode.

Writing port-check fallback logic...

I settle on printing a single plain URL line to stdout once the server binds in local mode, using the configured hostname so users immediately see where the app is running.

For README, I'm drafting the minimal judge quick-start: run npm ci, start OpenCode serve on a fixed port in one terminal, then npm start in another which prints the ready URL, and connect in the wizard using the password OpenCode prints. I'm still weighing whether to mention the hosted Render instance behind Basic auth, since credentials would need to be shared separately — I don't want to hardcode placeholder credentials into the README.

I also need to update docs/LOCAL_SETUP.md and several other files replacing the old port 4200 with 4310 — README, setup.ts, .env.example, config.ts, vite.config.ts — doing a careful search-and-replace since the context in each spot (like "port already in use" messages) stays valid either way. I'll leave the "stop dev servers first" note alone since that's a separate lower-priority item, and confirm no tests hardcode 4200 before running typecheck and tests.

I realize the user's local .env sets UB_PORT=4210 for the dev stack, which could conflict with the default when running npm start, but since Node's --env-file doesn't override existing shell env vars, I can safely verify by running with UB_PORT=4310 explicitly set in the shell without touching the gitignored .env file.

Writing port-check function...

I'm writing a helper that checks if OpenCode's health endpoint is reachable, but worry a plain 404 check could misfire if another server occupies the port — tightening the check to accept 200 OK or 401/403 auth responses instead. I'm also planning tests for portIsFree and openCodeReachable to cover both free and occupied ports.

Now I'm rewriting start.ts to validate the port and OpenCode reachability before launching, printing a clear error or warning if either check fails, then dynamically importing the main server module. I'm also adding a startup message printing the ready URL once the server binds, and noting that the wizard flow needs to surface OpenCode's terminal password to the user. Time to actually write the launch-check module.

The old port 4200 appears in the config, `.env.example`, `vite.config.ts`, the README, `LOCAL_SETUP.md`, and the web setup copy. Two details matter for the plan:
- Your local `.env` sets `UB_PORT=4210`, and `npm start` reads `.env`, so the new default will not apply on your machine unless you change `.env` or pass `UB_PORT`.
- The launcher should fail with a clear message when the port is busy, and warn when OpenCode is not reachable.

I'll add a small launch-check module for the port and OpenCode checks, then wire it into `start.ts`.

For judge instructions, I'll add a "Judge quick start" section in README covering the one-command start, the URL, the OpenCode step, and the deployed Render URL with a note about Basic auth credentials that the user needs to decide on. The live Render deployment already works fine, so no changes needed there.

I checked that tests don't reference the old port 4200, so that's safe. Now I'm designing the start.ts preflight logic: checking if the port is free by attempting to listen on it, and if it's busy, using a system command to identify the process holding it before printing a clear error and exiting. I'm also adding a quick health check against the OpenCode base URL with a short timeout, printing a warning if it's unreachable.

For the port and OpenCode checks, I confirmed start.ts is distinct from the Render startup path, so these preflight checks only affect local `npm start`/`dev` usage, which is correct. I'll also add a simple printed URL message when running in local mode so judges know where to open the browser, using plain stdout output rather than the structured JSON logging the rest of the app uses. The npm start script already chains the vite build step before launching the server, and building without a Sentry auth token should still work fine since it did before.

Now I'm writing the updated start.ts: wrapping config loading and the new preflight logic (checking if the port is free by probing it with a temporary server, plus pinging OpenCode's health endpoint) inside the existing try/catch, after the Sentry instrumentation import but before anything that depends on config being valid.

I decide a response status under 500 counts as reachable since even an auth failure means the server is listening, and I only need this check in local mode since hosted deployments spawn the server themselves. I'm organizing these checks into a separate launch-check module for testability, planning small tests for port and reachability detection, then sketching the start.ts flow that loads config and verifies the port is free before launching in local mode.

Writing port-check fallback logic...

I settle on printing a single plain URL line to stdout once the server binds in local mode, using the configured hostname so users immediately see where the app is running.

For README, I'm drafting the minimal judge quick-start: run npm ci, start OpenCode serve on a fixed port in one terminal, then npm start in another which prints the ready URL, and connect in the wizard using the password OpenCode prints. I'm still weighing whether to mention the hosted Render instance behind Basic auth, since credentials would need to be shared separately — I don't want to hardcode placeholder credentials into the README.

I also need to update docs/LOCAL_SETUP.md and several other files replacing the old port 4200 with 4310 — README, setup.ts, .env.example, config.ts, vite.config.ts — doing a careful search-and-replace since the context in each spot (like "port already in use" messages) stays valid either way. I'll leave the "stop dev servers first" note alone since that's a separate lower-priority item, and confirm no tests hardcode 4200 before running typecheck and tests.

I realize the user's local .env sets UB_PORT=4210 for the dev stack, which could conflict with the default when running npm start, but since Node's --env-file doesn't override existing shell env vars, I can safely verify by running with UB_PORT=4310 explicitly set in the shell without touching the gitignored .env file.

Writing port-check function...

I'm writing a helper that checks if OpenCode's health endpoint is reachable, but worry a plain 404 check could misfire if another server occupies the port — tightening the check to accept 200 OK or 401/403 auth responses instead. I'm also planning tests for portIsFree and openCodeReachable to cover both free and occupied ports.

Now I'm rewriting start.ts to validate the port and OpenCode reachability before launching, printing a clear error or warning if either check fails, then dynamically importing the main server module. I'm also adding a startup message printing the ready URL once the server binds, and noting that the wizard flow needs to surface OpenCode's terminal password to the user. Time to actually write the launch-check module.

The old port 4200 appears in the config, `.env.example`, `vite.config.ts`, the README, `LOCAL_SETUP.md`, and the web setup copy. Two details matter for the plan:
- Your local `.env` sets `UB_PORT=4210`, and `npm start` reads `.env`, so the new default will not apply on your machine unless you change `.env` or pass `UB_PORT`.
- The launcher should fail with a clear message when the port is busy, and warn when OpenCode is not reachable.

I'll add a small launch-check module for the port and OpenCode checks, then wire it into `start.ts`.

## Run it locally (judge path)

Prerequisites: Linux x64 or macOS, Node 22.14+, and npm.

```bash
# Terminal 1: OpenCode. Keep it running. Note the server password it prints.
npx --no-install opencode serve --hostname 127.0.0.1 --port 4096

# Terminal 2: the app. Builds the interface, then serves it and the API.
npm ci
npm start
```

Open the URL the app prints, `http://127.0.0.1:4310/`. The landing page and the recorded sample at `/demo` need nothing else. For a live run, open `/workshop`, connect to OpenCode with the password from Terminal 1, and choose a model. If the port is busy, `npm start` names the process holding it. Set `UB_PORT` in `.env` to use another port.

An optional USD session spending limit can be set, and the deployment can impose a stricter `UB_MAX_SESSION_COST_USD` ceiling.
